title: Rain barrels, cisterns and old water collection
h1: Rain barrels and cisterns: what the old records show, and why rainwater is not drinking water
dek: Jefferson's leaking cisterns, a fort that kept rain for fire, and a fortress cistern the Army feared. What the record shows about catching rain, and what the CDC and EPA say you need before anyone drinks it.
description: Historical rainwater collection at Monticello, Fort Union and San Juan, and the CDC and EPA position: rainwater is not safe to drink without testing and treatment.
recheck: If the CDC or EPA revise their rainwater or cistern pages, or when the primary records behind the site accounts (Jefferson's papers, Fort Union quartermaster records) are read directly.

source_use.hist-home-cdc-rainwater: Rainwater not necessarily safe to drink; sources of germs and chemicals; limit swallowing; test and treat; keep separate from piped water; first-flush diverters; mosquito cautions; local rules.
source_use.hist-home-cdc-cisterns: Untreated catchment cisterns after a disaster; disinfecting storm debris or floodwater does not work well; fuel and chemicals cannot be treated away; flush-only use.
source_use.hist-home-epa-rain-barrels: Rain barrels and cisterns defined; roof runoff can carry bacteria and chemicals; consider before using on edible plants.
source_use.cdc-find-clean-water: Rainwater and other outdoor sources must be treated.
source_use.hist-home-monticello-cisterns: Jefferson's four brick cisterns, his arithmetic, the leaks, and his unrealized sand-well plan for potable water.
source_use.hist-home-nps-fort-union-water: Fort Union's roof-fed cisterns kept for fire; wells and privies; the page is silent on drinking cistern water.
source_use.hist-home-nps-san-juan-cisterns: Spanish cisterns at San Juan, the 1898 closure on fear of poisoning, and restoration for non-potable use.
